image.altEn: Spanish-language xkcd comic #278: Black Hat Support

titleText.es: Para no dejaros con la intriga: era un problema con llamadas select()
titleText.en: So as not to leave you hanging: it was a problem with select() calls.

regions.labelEs: GRACIAS POR LLAMAR A LA LÍNEA DE SOPORTE DE BLACK HAT, SU PRIMERA FUENTE DE SOPORTE DE LINUX. ¿CÓMO PUEDO AYUDARLE?

excludedUnits.rationale: This is the English proper name of the support line and character, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Gracias supplies the thanks, por introduces its reason, and llamar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Le is attached to the unchanged verb ayudar and identifies the formal listener receiving the help.

regions.labelEs: HOLA. ESTOY CORRIENDO UN SERVIDOR APACHE Y LA CARGA NO PARA DE SUBIR SIN CONTROL.

applications.explanationEn: Estoy identifies the speaker and corriendo supplies the ongoing action form ending in -iendo.
No negates para, de links it to the continuing action, and subir stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Sin and control form the fixed description for a change that is no longer controlled.

regions.labelEs: VALE. PRIMER PULSE EN EL MENÚ INICIO.

applications.explanationEn: Pulse is the polite command form addressed to one formal usted listener.

regions.labelEs: PERDÓN, ESTO ES LA LÍNEA DE AYUDA DE LINUX, ¿VERDAD?

applications.explanationEn: Por and supuesto work together as the conventional expression for confident agreement.
The unspoken subject is formal usted, so abre uses the same singular form used with él or ella.

regions.labelEs: UN MOMENTO. CREO QUE SE ESÁ QUEDANDO CONMIGO.

applications.explanationEn: Un momento interrupts the exchange and asks the other speaker to pause.
The printed esá is a misspelling of the intended auxiliary está, while quedando supplies the ongoing action form ending in -ando.
Se and quedando form the relevant use of quedarse, while conmigo identifies the person who suspects he is being fooled.
Disculpe is the polite command form for one formal listener, with me attached at the end.

regions.labelEs: AHORA ABRA SU AOL Y VAYA A LA PALABRA CLAVE "LINUX"...

applications.explanationEn: Abra is the polite command form addressed to one formal usted listener.
Vaya is the irregular polite command form used to direct one formal listener.
Palabra and clave form the conventional compound for a term used to search or gain access.

cards.questionEn: How do you thank someone for doing something?
cards.answerEn: Say gracias por, then put the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Por introduces the reason for the thanks. The following action stays in the dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, even where English uses a verb ending in -ing.

cards.answerEn: for (introducing what someone is thanked for)
no separate English word; links llamar to the person, number, or service called
no separate English word; links an item to its type
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between an item and the noun that identifies its type. English often puts the type noun first instead: libro de historia becomes “history book.”
With formal usted, su can mean “your.” The same form can also mean “his,” “her,” or “their,” so context identifies the owner.

cards.answerEn: for; links support or help to the system it covers

cards.promptEs: Apache y Linux frente a Menú Inicio, Mis Documentos y AOL
cards.answerEn: Apache can run as a web server on Linux, while Start and My Documents are Windows interface names and AOL Keywords belonged to AOL. Those steps do not address the caller's Linux server problem.
cards.noteEn: The Black Hat character deliberately gives obsolete, mismatched consumer-computer instructions. The growing mismatch is the central support-call joke.
Ayudar is the unchanged dictionary form, and le means the formal listener here. Spanish attaches le to the end of an unchanged verb and writes ayudarle as one word.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

cards.noteEn: Correr usually describes running on foot, but in technology it can describe operating software, a process, or a server.

cards.answerEn: load; demand on a computer system
cards.noteEn: In computing, carga describes how much work the system is handling rather than a physical weight.

example.es: La carga del sistema es alta.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something keeps doing an action without stopping?
cards.answerEn: Use no, then a changed form of parar, then de, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Only parar changes for the person and time. The action after de stays in its dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Although the words literally say that the action does not stop, natural English often uses “keep doing.”

example.es: El bebé no para de reír.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links parar to the action that stops

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is uncontrolled or out of control?
cards.noteEn: Sin means “without,” so sin control can describe movement or change that is no longer controlled. English may use “out of control” or an adverb such as “uncontrollably.”

example.en: The car spins out of control.

cards.answerEn: first; printed before a verb where standard Spanish would use primero
cards.noteEn: Primer is the shortened form of primero used before a masculine singular noun, as in el primer paso. Before an instruction verb such as pulse, standard Spanish uses primero instead. The comic visibly prints primer.

cards.answerEn: Use the usted command form: regular -ar verbs end in -e, while regular -er and -ir verbs end in -a.
cards.noteEn: Usted is the polite or formal singular “you.” Hablar becomes hable, comer becomes coma, and escribir becomes escriba. Usted is usually left out because the command ending already shows formal address. Some common verbs are irregular, such as decir → diga.
cards.questionEn: How do you politely tell one person to do something in Spanish?

cards.noteEn: Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por supuesto (“of course”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say “of course” when something is obvious or agreed?
cards.noteEn: Por supuesto is a fixed expression. It can confirm a request or emphasize that the speaker sees something as expected.

example.en: Of course, you can come in.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por supuesto (“of course”)
you open (formal singular, in an if-clause)
Use the same singular verb form used with él or ella (“he” or “she”).
cards.noteEn: Although usted refers to the listener, Spanish treats it like “he” or “she” when choosing the verb. Compare tú necesitas for informal “you need” with usted necesita for formal “you need.” Spanish often leaves usted unspoken when the context makes it clear.
cards.questionEn: When usted means polite or formal “you,” which verb form goes with it?
What does ¡Un momento! mean when someone interrupts or suddenly realizes something?
cards.answerEn: It means “Wait a moment!” or “Hold on!”
cards.noteEn: This fixed conversational interruption can ask someone to pause, or it can announce that the speaker has just noticed something important. Its function is broader than literally measuring one moment.

example.es: ¡Un momento! Creo que tengo la llave.
example.en: Hold on! I think I have the key.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks the idiom quedarse con alguien

cards.promptEs: quedarse con alguien para bromear o engañar
cards.questionEn: How can you say that someone is teasing, fooling, or putting another person on?
cards.answerEn: In Spain, use a form of quedarse con followed by the person being teased or fooled.
cards.noteEn: The small pronoun in quedarse changes with the person doing it: me, te, se, nos, or os. Context matters because quedarse con can also literally mean to keep something or stay with someone. In this idiomatic use, it describes not speaking sincerely to the other person.

example.es: No te quedes conmigo; dime la verdad.
example.en: Don't mess with me; tell me the truth.

cards.answerEn: you are; printed misspelling of está
cards.noteEn: The visible word omits the t from está but keeps the accent on á. The intended está is the form used with formal usted and helps form an ongoing action.

cards.answerEn: teasing; fooling (as part of quedarse con alguien)
please excuse me; bear with me (formal)
cards.noteEn: Disculpe is a polite command to one person, and me means “me.” In a positive command, Spanish attaches me to the end and writes discúlpeme as one word; the accent keeps the original stress.

example.en: Excuse me, can you repeat that?

cards.questionEn: How do you say “keyword” or “key term” in Spanish?
cards.noteEn: Palabra names the word, and clave says it is important for access, searching, or identifying a topic. The common plural is palabras clave.

cards.answerEn: key; keyword (as part of palabra clave)
